title: The Stations of the Cross
hookLine: fourteen stops along the way of the cross, prayed in some churches

cards: Along the side walls of some churches hang small carvings or paintings, spaced out like mile markers. A man standing before a judge. A woman holding out a cloth.
A stranger pulled from the crowd to carry a beam of wood. On Good Friday, and in some churches on other Fridays too, people walk from one to the next. They stop, they pray, they move on.

In Jerusalem, pilgrims walk a route through the old streets that tradition calls the way of sorrows, stopping at the same scenes. On a church wall, the walk comes to wherever you live. Today, the Stations of the Cross.

teach.b: The stations are a walk with stops. Tradition counts fourteen in the usual set, from Jesus condemned to his body laid in the tomb. Some come straight from the Gospels; others come from tradition.
Take one from the Gospels first. Luke says that as they led Jesus away, the soldiers grabbed a passerby.

teach.h: SIMON, TO BEAR IT AFTER JESUS.
teach.b: In the King James: "they laid hold upon one Simon, a Cyrenian, coming out of the country, and on him they laid the cross, that he might bear it after Jesus."
A man on his way into the city ends up walking directly behind Jesus with the weight on his shoulders. Some readers hear in that phrase, after Jesus, the language of following.
A little further on, Luke has women in the crowd weeping, and Jesus turns to them: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not for me, but weep for yourselves, and for your children."
Even on that road he turns to face them, and his words point past his own suffering to troubles still ahead for the city and its children.
Other stations, like Jesus falling under the cross, or a woman named Veronica wiping his face, come from tradition rather than the Gospel text.
The stations are prayed in Catholic and Anglican churches, and in some others.

teach.h: SOME FROM THE GOSPELS, SOME FROM TRADITION.
teach.b: Some versions use only scenes found in the Gospels, and some Protestants prefer it that way. Whichever set is used, the shape is the same: you walk a few steps, stop at one moment, stay with it, then walk again.

how: Catholics, Anglicans and some other Christians pray the Stations of the Cross, especially on Good Friday, walking from station to station in church with a short reading and prayer at each.

games.q: you're Simon, coming into the city from the country. soldiers grab you out of the crowd. what happens next?
o: they lay the cross on you, and you carry it behind Jesus.
they send you to fetch water.
games.why: Luke: "on him they laid the cross, that he might bear it after Jesus." a stranger ends up walking right behind him.

practice: Walk slowly around the room, down a hallway, or in place, and stop now and then for one breath, fourteen times if you like, without counting too carefully.
At each stop, let one face come to mind, someone carrying something heavy right now, and hold them there for a breath the way Simon held the beam; if you pray, name each one to God.

wordCard.voice: Cyrenian. The name for Simon, the passerby soldiers pulled from the crowd to carry Jesus's cross, walking it one station at a time.

orig.note: Greek: cross — the word in Luke 23:26, where the cross is laid on Simon.

carryVoice: Your line: step by step with him. One stop, then the next. See you tomorrow.
